questiontext.text: Which data structure does breadth-first search use to decide the order in which vertices are explored?

feedback.text: Correct — a queue processes vertices in the order they were discovered, level by level.
A stack gives depth-first order, not breadth-first.

answer.text: A min-priority queue keyed by edge weight

feedback.text: That describes Dijkstra or Prim, not plain BFS.
Union-find is used by Kruskal's MST, not by BFS.

generalfeedback.text: BFS enqueues a vertex when first discovered and dequeues in FIFO order, so vertices are visited in non-decreasing distance from the source.

questiontext.text: On which kind of graph does BFS from a source vertex compute a shortest path (fewest edges) to every reachable vertex?

answer.text: An unweighted graph (or one where every edge has equal weight)

feedback.text: Correct — with uniform edge cost, level order equals shortest-path order.

answer.text: Any weighted graph with arbitrary positive weights

feedback.text: No — with unequal weights you need Dijkstra; BFS counts edges, not weight.
BFS works on cyclic and undirected graphs too; the key restriction is unweighted edges.
Completeness is irrelevant; edge weighting is what matters.

generalfeedback.text: Because BFS expands vertices in order of edge-distance, the first time it reaches a vertex it has used the fewest possible edges — a shortest path when all edges cost the same.

questiontext.text: Using an adjacency list, what is the time complexity of BFS on a graph with V vertices and E edges?

feedback.text: Correct — each vertex is enqueued once and each edge is examined once.
O(V^2) arises with an adjacency matrix, not with an adjacency list.
That is Prim/Dijkstra with a heap; BFS uses a plain queue.
BFS is linear in the graph size, not factorial.

generalfeedback.text: With an adjacency list every vertex and every edge is touched a constant number of times, giving O(V + E).

questiontext.text: Why does BFS mark vertices with a visited (or discovered) set?

answer.text: To avoid enqueuing the same vertex twice and prevent infinite loops on cycles

feedback.text: Correct — without it, a cycle would re-add vertices forever.

answer.text: To sort the vertices by weight before traversal

feedback.text: BFS does not sort by weight; it processes in discovery order.

answer.text: To guarantee the graph is a tree

feedback.text: The visited set lets BFS handle general graphs; it does not require a tree.
The queue, not the visited set, controls order; marking is only about correctness.

generalfeedback.text: Marking a vertex when discovered ensures each vertex is processed exactly once, so BFS terminates even on graphs with cycles.

questiontext.text: BFS visits all neighbors of a vertex before moving on to vertices that are farther from the source.

feedback.text: Correct — BFS explores level by level, finishing distance d before starting distance d+1.
This is exactly the defining behavior of BFS.

questiontext.text: Plain BFS always finds the minimum-weight path in a graph with arbitrary positive edge weights.

feedback.text: No — BFS minimizes the number of edges, not total weight; use Dijkstra for weighted graphs.
Correct — BFS is only shortest-path-optimal when edges are unweighted or all equal.

questiontext.text: BFS manages its frontier of vertices to visit next using a FIFO ______ (single English word).

feedback.text: Correct — a FIFO queue drives the level-order traversal.
Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about breadth-first search are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It runs in O(V + E) with an adjacency list

feedback.text: Yes — linear in vertices plus edges.

answer.text: It finds shortest paths by edge count in an unweighted graph

feedback.text: Yes — level order gives fewest-edge paths.

answer.text: It uses a stack and backtracks to go as deep as possible

feedback.text: No — that describes DFS, not BFS.

answer.text: It requires edge weights to be sorted before it can start

feedback.text: No — BFS ignores weights entirely.

generalfeedback.text: BFS is a queue-based, O(V + E) traversal that yields fewest-edge shortest paths in unweighted graphs; depth-first behavior and weight sorting belong to other algorithms.
